newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's MRTA - the gentlemen guerrillas?.
newsitem.headline: Peru's MRTA - the gentlemen guerrillas?.

text.p: It is not often that a group of gun-toting hostage-takers have received such glowing praise.
Almost to a man, captives released by about 20 Marxist guerrillas from the Japanese ambassador's residence in Peru have painted a picture of determined but decent young rebels.

Psychologists say hostages held for long periods often end up sympathising with their captors. But in Lima hostages released on Sunday praised the gunmen after just five days of captivity. More than half of the 225 men set free as a Christmas goodwill gesture shook hands with the gunmen as they left, some even wishing them good luck, Canadian oil executive Kieran Metcalfe said.

Soon after their spectacular assault on the Japanese ambassador's elegant cocktail party on Dec. 17 the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels released all women, including President Alberto Fujimori's mother and sister, citing humanitarian motives.

After the tension of the first night, fears about the hostages' safety eased as emerging captives gave glowing reports of their treatment. Looking tired but well, they told reporters they were not harmed physically or abused verbally by the rebels.
"This has been an excellent propaganda coup for them, which was clearly one of their main objectives," university professor Carlos Aquino Rodriguez told Reuters hours after his release on Sunday.

Apart from a brief shootout with police shortly after the assault, which left at least one of the rebels with a bullet wound, no blood was shed. An ultimatum to begin killing hostages on the second day, starting with Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, passed without incident and was not repeated.
Indeed, despite living under the watchful eye of well-armed gunmen, most hostages have said they feared an assault from outside more than violence from the guerrillas.

"I don't think that you'll see any of them taking anyone's life and throwing a body out the front door and saying, you know, 'There will be one in another hour unless things happen,'" Kris Merschrod, a freed U.S. sociologist, told CBS Evening News.
Hostages said the rebels allowed them to talk freely and circulate inside the two-floor residence. The guerrillas laid no special claim to scarce food and water resources.
"You can walk up to them and say 'Hey man, I have a question, I want to use the bathroom, is that all right?' and they'd say 'Go right ahead,'" Merschrod said.

Nestor Cerpa, the textile factory worker turned revolutionary who led Tuesday's daring attack, has also won respect from his former captives. "He explained his strategy and what his movement wanted ... My personal opinion is that he is a cultured man, well-read and quite intelligent," Aquino said.
Cerpa organised roundtable discussions to explain the rebels' cause and took great pains to ensure that, as he put it, captives "are leaving with a different idea of what the MRTA is."
Smaller and less well known than the Maoist Shining Path rebel group, the MRTA emerged in the 1980s as a Robin Hood-style movement that hijacked trucks and distributed goods to peasants.
"They have always used their brains. They are intelligent, much more intelligent than Shining Path, who just kill everybody and damage everything," Lima taxi driver Ricardo Mendes said.

The treatment received inside the besieged ambassador's home has left many ex-hostages optimistic about a peaceful end to the crisis. "These people have an angle. Their angle basically is that they want to be part of the political process and I'm really optimistic that this thing will be resolved by negotiation, not by force," Merschrod said.
